abstract_text: 25 years of Basking Shark watch sightings have revealed considerable spatio-temporal trends of shark occurrence in the British Isles. Hotspots of shark sightings persist in the Southwest, Isle of Man and western Scotland. The treatment of the data to reduce the impact of observer bias has shown that strong North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) years are persistent with longer Basking Shark surface sightings seasons, and that sea surface temperature (SST) appears to be the key signal of the onset of Basking Shark surface feeding. Other research has suggested that a reduction in surface plankton concentration appears to lead to the tailing off of the Basking Shark sightings. Concomitant conservation work focused around the UK Biodiversity Action Plan for the species has led to the successful annexation of the species on the Bonn Convention of Migratory Species since tagging studies have proven international migrations of the species. Although there has been considerable progress in the conservation and knowledge of essential habitat requirements of the species at different spatial scales, fundamental questions such as population numbers, and population trends are still beyond us. Despite these issues, an international Basking Shark conference on the Isle of Man in 2009 recommended that the database is continued, because of its long-term spatio-temporal time series. It demonstrates that public sightings schemes have considerable worth when combined with rigorous scientific research, and applied conservation work.

title: Diel patterns in vertical movement and locomotor activity of Whale Sharks at Ningaloo Reef

authors.affiliation: Bioscience, College of Science, Swansea University

abstract_text: Activity patterns of animals often relate to environmental variables such as food availability and predation pressure. Technological advances are providing us with new tools to monitor and better understand these activity patterns. We used animal-attached data loggers recording acceleration and depth to compare activity patterns and vertical habitat use of Whale Sharks Rhincodon typus at Ningaloo Reef, Western Australia. Whale Sharks showed a moderate reverse diel vertical migration but exhibited a clear crepuscular pattern in locomotory activity. Peak activity occurred at sunset, whereas vertical movement peaked prior to this. Typical ram surface filter feeding could be identified and occurred primarily during sunset and the first hours of night. At such times, direct observations indicated whale sharks were feeding on tropical krill swarms. Diel patterns in activity and diving suggest that whale sharks have tuned their diving behaviour in anticipation of the formation of these high-density patches which appear to only be periodically, but predictably available at sunset. Our results confirm that diel patterns in vertical habitat selection and vertical movements do not necessarily reflect patterns in activity and foraging behaviour. Direct quantification of activity and behaviour is required in gaining accurate representation of diel activity patterns. We also note that by combining behavioural tracking with environmental monitoring we can start to identify and map regions of seasonal importance, including hotspots for feeding and spawning for example.

abstract_text: Reliable abundance assessments are essential to the study of population dynamics and underpin conservation biology and management of a species. Although fishing pressure is a major threat to manta spp., information on the trends and status of many of the species’ subpopulations is lacking. Here we use photographic identification and mark-recapture methods to report on the site affinity, size and structure of an unexploited subpopulation of Manta alfredi in eastern Australian waters. A total of 716 individuals were identified between 2007 and 2012, including 636 at Lady Elliot Island (LEI), southern Great Barrier Reef. Over 60% of individuals were resighted at least once during the study period. Multiple resightings within and among years imply a high degree of site affinity to aggregation sites by individuals. One individual was sighted 11 times at LEI within a 27-year period. The sex ratio of this manta ray subpopulation was significantly biased toward females with an overall 1.3:1 female-to-male ratio. Overall, females were more likely to be resighted than males, however, site visitation at LEI varied between sexes. Robust design population models were used to estimate the population size of the winter aggregation at LEI over a 4-year period. The model estimated up to 532 individuals in the population within one winter season and that survivorship of M. alfredi between consecutive years was exceptionally high (φ~1). Our findings highlighted the importance of aggregation sites for M. alfredi subpopulations, and provide a valuable baseline to assist in the status assessment of exploited manta ray subpopulations.

title: Vertical foraging strategies of Basking Sharks in coastal waters and their implication for population surveys

authors.affiliation: Queens University Belfast / Irish Basking Shark Study Group
Queens University Belfast / Irish Basking Shark Study Group
Queens University Belfast / Irish Basking Shark Study Group

abstract_text: The adoption of the distance sampling survey method for estimating Basking Shark density and relative abundance has proven difficult because estimates of time at the surface, under varying conditions, are poorly understood (Sims et al., 2003; Southall et al., 2005; Campana, 2008). Here we explore how variance in vertical prey (zooplankton) distribution under different sea states account for variance in the period of time sharks spend in the top metre of the water column where they are detectable during surveys. Vertical prey distribution was recorded by variable depth sampling (1-30 metres) across a grid of nine coastal sample sites located at Malin Head, Ireland. Zooplankton samples were taken via Von Dorn Bottle and vertical plankton net hauls during calm (Force 0-2) and moderate (Force 3-4) conditions. Shark positions throughout the water column (i.e. depth) were determined at one second intervals using CEFAS G5 Time Depth Recorders (TDR’s) attached for 1-6 days (N=11 sharks). By considering the vertical movements of predators concurrent with estimates of prey field and weather we determined survey weightings applicable to mixed coastal water habitats during calm and moderate conditions.

title: Basking Sharks and oceanic fronts: remotely-sensed ocean front metrics for improving understanding of marine megavertebrate habitat use

authors.affiliation: Plymouth Marine Laboratory, UK
Plymouth Marine Laboratory, UK

abstract_text: Oceanic fronts delineate between water masses, manifesting as enhanced horizontal gradients in temperature, salinity, density, turbidity or colour. Bio-physical coupling along fronts can drive the formation of pelagic foraging hotspots. Many, taxonomically diverse marine vertebrates are known to associate with fronts, including several pelagic sharks and the giant manta Manta birostris. For example, the planktivorous Basking Shark Cetorhinus maximus is known to exploit rich foraging opportunities afforded by zooplankton aggregation along fronts over a range of spatial scales. Recent advances in remote sensing, coupled with animal tracking/biologging, can now generate high-resolution, individual-level insights into the physical drivers of habitat selection. Composite front mapping enables objective detection of thermal and chlorophyll-a fronts and the derivation of metrics quantifying frontal activity in an animal’s proximal environment. Use of these methods has improved understanding of levels of association between basking sharks and fronts in the North Atlantic. Our findings show strong associations in some cases, with sharks following the surface profile of thermal fronts for several days. Recent collaborative work also identifies persistent open ocean frontal zones as a ‘front line’ in shark conservation, as hotspots of overlap between high-use habitat and intensive pelagic longlining activity. Broad-scale, objective detection of frontal zones and their spatiotemporal dynamics could help in identification of priority conservation areas in the open oceans, where sharks and rays remain largely unprotected from deleterious interactions with anthropogenic activity.

title: Evidence of sexual conflict in Potamotrygon motoro Chondrichthyes-Potamotrygonidae at Rio Negro Basin

authors.affiliation: DIMAR-UFRPE
DIMAR-UFRPE
DIMAR-UFRPE

abstract_text: Potamotrygon motoro (Müller & Henle, 1841) is a freshwater stingray member of Potamotrygonidae family. It exhibits a wide distribution in the Neotropical Region. At Rio Negro basin, Amazonas State, Brazil, this species reach sexual maturity with 39.0-42.00 cm disc width, 4-5 years. The reproductive cycle events (mate, ovulation, gestation and birth) are regulated by the level of the river. Dermal bites wounds are visible in female and male skins during the dry season. In the complex reproductive behaviour of elasmobranchs male bites female as a precopulatory mechanism to have female acquiescence during courtship. Records were done of females bit the mating males, and the authors suggest a sexual hierarchy during the copulation event. To understand the meaning of male dermal bites of P. motoro from Rio Negro basin, 65 adult male skin were analysed and compare with teeth morphology of male and female tooth forms. Ours results indicate that P. motoro has teeth sexually dimorphic, females teeth with rhombic posterior margin, mature males with cuspidate posterior margin. All scars in male skins were impressions of male cuspidate form of teeth. Despite the adult sexual ratio at mate area be 1:1, these findings suggest the occurrence of male dispute during the mating season of Potamotrygon motoro at Rio Negro basin.

title: Shark hand signals for shark identification

authors.affiliation: Shark Academy, Italy

abstract_text: Hand signals are the common way for scuba divers and swimmers to communicate underwater. Divers use signals for emergency purposes, routine communication and for general reasons such as to indicate a marine life form to the buddy. This communication method has multiple advantages: it is simple, effective and easy to use. Each signal is characterized by a gesture, which immediately identifies the shark in question. It refers to gestures one can make with one or two hands and are completed by the position of the arm. These signals let one not only communicate the type of shark which is coming close, but also to know in which direction to look. As a matter of fact, if a seabed shark is signalled (benthonic) the diver will look among the rocks and not upwards, as instead one would if it referred to a surface shark (pelagic). The information therefore supplies, the position of the shark, and would not only be used in case of danger, but having once checked the shark species, the diver could decide to avoid the wrong type of behaviour, with incorrect movements, inciting the shark to attack, but would also make taking photos and filming easier, as well as confirming the precise identification or a useless encounter in the case of uncertainty. It is important to be able to directly encounter the shark head on if one is trying to identify it and to get out of the water with both the same opinion about the sighting: this lets one be more precise in filling in any identification file. To know the movements of differing shark species and their habitat, gives indirect information about the whole marine ecosystem.

abstract_text: The influence of maturity stage and age on the bathymetric distribution of Longnosed Skate Dipturus oxyrinchus (Linnaeus, 1758) in the Sardinian seas was investigated. Since 2005 to 2012, a total of 494 (266 females and 228 males) individuals, from 15.7 and 115.5 cm TL, were caught during experimental and commercial trawl surveys at depths between 129 and 650m. Each individual was measured and weighted. Maturity stages were attributed following the MEDITS scales for the Elasmobranchs. The age was evaluated through the count of vertebral centra’s annuli from a subsample of 75 females and 53 males. The VBGF parameters were determined (L∞ = 149.2, s.e.= 15.72; k = 0.08, s.e. = 0.02; t0 = -0.8, s.e. = 0.29 and L∞ = 118.97, s.e. = 10.82; k = 0.11, s.e. = 0.02; t0 = -1.08, s.e. = 0.32 for females and males, respectively). ANOSIM showed differences (global R = 0.136, p<0.001) among the six considered strata (A to F with intervals of 100m). Upper than 300m (A and B strata) were mostly found immature individuals from 3+ to 6+ and specimens ≥12+ at maturity stage 2 and 3 for females and males, respectively. Between 300-500m (C-D strata), the population was composed almost exclusively by immature skates <5+. Over 500m (E-F) younger immatures (<3+) of both sexes and older females (>12+, stage 3 and 4) were mainly present. D. oxyrinchus seems to mate in shallower waters. After that, females migrate to deeper strata to spawn, while younger individuals carry out a reverse migration during growth.

abstract_text: The Pelagic Thresher Shark Alopias pelagicus is one of the largest and most abundant open ocean predators in the Eastern Tropical Pacific (ETP), and one of the most exploited shark in the sub-region. A. pelagicus has been classified as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List since 2004. Since 1994, there have been a progressive reduction of the landed volumes and the average size of captures. This information is a serious concern; given the number of people who depend on fishing in this area and the ecological repercussions linked to top elasmobranchs decrease. Nonetheless, little is known about the biology and ecology of this species and the pelagic thresher shark is consequently recognized has the highest priority species for management in the Colombian (Shark NPOA) which various time series research activities for the study of its biology and ecology. Short-term research activities include the study of the migrations and movement patterns along the Pacific Coast while population genetics are identified as long-term activities both selected DRDH with the Foundation Malpelo and the Ministry of Fisheries of Colombia (AUNAP), created in 2012 the COLSHARK program to study this specie. One of the objectives was to organize for the first time in the ETP, a scientific fishery expedition to tag Pelagic Thresher Sharks off Pacific Colombian coasts. The 10 days expedition took place in March 2013 in Baya Solano (El Choco area) 11 satellite mini PAT tags and 20 visual tags were successfully deployed. After 6 months, 10 satellite tags have been released and DRDH is able to present some preliminary results on Alopias pelagicus movement patterns in ETP.

abstract_text: Basking Sharks are considered Endangered in the Northeast Atlantic, but the size of this population is uncertain. We used photo-identification to investigate their abundance both in a focal study area (the islands of Mull, Coll and Tiree on Scotland’s west coast), and over the larger region probably incorporating the whole western British Isles. In our focal area, from a total of 793 photographed encounters, 615 sharks were found to have distinguishing features, but, of these, only 35 individuals were re-sighted. Most were re-sighted within 1-3 days but only a few between years. We did obtain sufficient re-sightings to generate reliable estimates for our small focal study area for two short periods, but the very low recapture rate between years precluded precise abundance estimates for the wider British Isles region. This low rate does however indicate a much larger regional population (up to 10,000 or more) than previously anticipated. To investigate these low recapture rates further, most recently we have repeated (in 2013) photo-identification of sharks in our focal area, and have also compared our pictures with those submitted to the Shark Trust photo-identification database by colleagues in England and Ireland. In all cases the proportion of re-sightings between different years and between different locations has proved to be only a few percent, indicating a regional (British Isles) population in the low tens of thousands. These data suggest that there may have been a significant recovery of the regional Basking Shark population since the 1980s when their exploitation ceased.

title: Mapping to manage: Irish Sea rays

authors.affiliation: Marine and Freshwater Research Centre, Galway-Mayo Institute of Technology

abstract_text: Poor or patchy data hamper better management of the Irish Sea assemblage of Cuckoo Ray Leucoraja naevus, Thornback Ray Raja clavata, Blonde Ray Raja brachyura, and Spotted Ray Raja montagui. Pursuing traditional stock assessments for these species is not possible: species-specific landings data are unavailable. Species misidentification, use of inappropriate survey gear, and variable availability of tagging, fecundity, and age data also preclude typical single-species assessment and management of these stocks. The most recent ICES advice recommends that a suite of species and fishery-specific measures be developed to address these problems, and to achieve recovery of the depleted species. The aim of this study is to synthesise numerous disparate datasets to describe the southern Irish Sea ray fishery, and highlight key areas that warrant protection as part of a future spatial management plan for the species assemblage. The datasets available include environmental (e.g. temperature, salinity, substrate, bathymetry, currents, etc.), biological (ICES surveys, existing scientifically derived species parameters), and fisheries data (landings, effort, discard, observer and eggcase data, economic and social assessment of the fishery). Appropriate data assimilation tools may include the MPA zoning software ‘MARXAN’, species distribution modelling ‘MaxEnt’, or the fish stock simulator ‘GislaSim’. Data deficiencies may also be filled by borrowing knowledge from similar, more data-rich stocks (the ‘Robin Hood’ approach). The research outputs are intended to improve spatial management by identifying areas of highest value as nurseries, or refugia containing high diversity.

title: Status, exploitation and management of Starry Smoothhound Mustelus asterias in the Northeast Atlantic

authors.affiliation: Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research (GEOMAR), Kiel, Germany

abstract_text: The Starry Smoothhound Mustelus asterias is classified as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. However catch rates have increased in recent years and therefore appropriate management is needed. Here the Northeast Atlantic stock was examined on the basis of ICES survey data, with respect to exploitation and abundance trends. Information on biology and life history was summarised from the literature, as well as partly recalculated by this study. The median of empirical equations drawing on growth parameters and age at maturity served as estimate of natural mortality. Total mortality was obtained from pooled catch-at-age data for two different time periods. Total mortality minus natural mortality was used as a proxy for fishing mortality. The results were compared with the fishing mortality that would produce maximum sustainable yield, defined as half the intrinsic rate of population increase. Recent and historical trends in CPUE were derived from abundance data (years 1992 to 2012). Relative exploitation levels from survey and catch data were examined from 1997 to 2011 and compared to a 1:1 replacement ratio. It is hoped that these results will help in sustainable management of this species.

title: Status, exploitation and management of Tope Galeorhinus galeus in the Northeast Atlantic

authors.affiliation: Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research (GEOMAR), Kiel, Germany

abstract_text: Tope Galeorhinus galeus is classified as Data Deficient on the IUCN Red List for the Northeast Atlantic, but its status is Vulnerable worldwide. Here, the Northeast Atlantic stock was examined with respect to exploitation and abundance trends. The study was based on ICES survey data. Information on biology and life history traits was summarised from the literature, as well as partly reanalysed by this study. A newly developed approach was applied to determine von Bertalanffy growth parameters from tagging data. The median of empirical equations drawing on growth parameters and age at maturity served as estimate of natural mortality. Total mortality was obtained from pooled catch-at-age data of a representative area. Total mortality minus natural mortality was used as a proxy for fishing mortality. The results were compared with the fishing mortality that would produce maximum sustainable yield, defined as half the intrinsic rate of population increase. Recent and historical trends in CPUE were derived from abundance data (years 1992 to 2012). Relative exploitation levels from survey and catch data were calculated for the time period 1997 to 2011 and compared to a 1:1 replacement ratio. Furthermore, the study shows that even with presumably sustainable fishing pressure, shark stocks can be severely overfished if fishing starts at early ages. It is hoped that this results will help in the sustainable management of this species.

title: Crossing paths: Marine Protected Areas and migratory sharks

authors.affiliation: Zoological Society of London
Zoological Society of London
Zoological Society of London
Zoological Society of London

abstract_text: The value of marine protected areas (MPAs) for the protection of marine species has been extensively cited. However, recent work on the protection of migratory species has called into question the effectiveness of the current MPA network in safeguarding these often critically endangered species. Highly migratory pelagic species, such as sharks, whales, and tuna, tend to have high aesthetic and/or commercial value, putting their protection at the forefront of conservation activity. While properly placed MPAs can contribute to the protection of migratory species, it is unclear how existing MPA networks overlap with migratory patterns of endangered species. A subset of sharks listed by the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS) and the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) was selected to determine how the distribution and presence of these species overlaps with global MPA coverage. The selection of these two conventions for this analysis is highly topical: CITES CoP16 occurred in March and the 11th CMS CoP will take place in 2014. Using the World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA) and shark range data, this study presents the overlap between distributions of endangered sharks with both general and ‘no-take’ MPAs. The data derived contribute to the understanding of the effectiveness of the current MPA network for migratory sharks in terms of locality and connectivity. Critical analysis of international progress towards marine protection targets will provide guidance for future MPA development, and identify possibilities for international cooperation in the conservation of migratory species.

abstract_text: The Thresher Shark Alopias vulpinus is a large top-predator showing a marked decline in the Mediterranean Sea. This species is considered critically endangered in Italian waters. This study focused on the occurrence and fishery of this species in the northern Adriatic Sea. Despite being not continuous, annual fishery data (1945-2012) from the fish market of Chioggia, (home to the major fishing fleet of the study area) highlighted a positive correlation between catches of Thresher and sardine (rS= + 0.47, p = 0.023, N = 31), while no correlation was found with anchovy (rS= + 0.18, p = 0.51, N = 31) or sea water temperature (rS= + 0.05, p = 0.81, N = 31). The correlation between Thresher and sardine suggests migrations of Threshers in the northern Adriatic according to prey availability. The estimated annual number of Threshers landed at the fish market (1997-2012) is 14 ±6, mainly caught in mid-water trawls from April to October. More than 30% of landed Threshers were below 10kg in eviscerated weight, with some specimens weighting less than 3kg, indicating a high proportion of catch composed by small young and newborn individuals. Surveys at the fish market highlighted the occurrence of both males and females.

title: Fishery and reproductive biology of Scyliorhinus canicula in the northern Adriatic

authors.affiliation: University of Padova
University of Padova
University of Padova
University of Padova

abstract_text: Scyliorhinus canicula is a small, benthic, oviparous species, inhabiting the Northeast Atlantic and the Mediterranean Sea. This study focuses on the fishery and reproductive biology of this species in the northern Adriatic Sea. Analysis of historical landings data from the fish market of Chioggia (the major market for the northern Adriatic) revealed a 89.4% decline in the capture of catsharks between the 1940s and 2012. This species is mainly captured as bycatch in beam trawls, especially from October to April. Data obtained from 188 surveys at the fish market (from January 2011 to June 2013) showed a sex-ratio biased towards female (male:female = 1:3.85). The catch was composed mainly of mature individuals (96% ±2 female; 97% ±3 male), ranging in size between 360 and 530mm (N = 1731). Females carrying egg capsules completely or partially formed were found throughout the year, suggesting a prolonged laying period. Length at first maturity was 370mm for males and 390mm for females. Estimates of fecundity (number of oocytes larger than 1.6mm) ranged from 32 to 124 and were positively correlated to female size (r = 0.40, p < 0.01; N = 98; female size: 390 – 48 mm total length). The decline in catch highlighted that even a small early maturing species can be severely depleted by fishery and/or other pressures and calls for management actions.

title: Does sperm competition influence sperm and genital evolution in sharks?

authors.affiliation: University of Manchester

abstract_text: Sperm competition, the contest among sperm from rival males to fertilize a female’s eggs, is a powerful selective force shaping the evolution of sperm traits and genital morphology in many taxa. Yet very little is known about how sperm competition influences sperm and genital morphology in sharks. However, recent research reveals that female multiple mating is common in sharks, which sets the stage for sperm competition, and that sharks exhibit tremendous diversity among species in sperm and genital morphology, a hallmark of the effects of sperm competition on the evolution of reproductive traits. Here I provide a preliminary assessment of the relevance of sperm competition as a selective force shaping sperm and genital evolution in sharks.

title: Public perceptions of sharks: investigating support for shark conservation

authors.affiliation: Centre for Marine and Coastal Policy, Marine Institute, Plymouth University
Centre for Marine and Coastal Policy, Marine Institute, Plymouth University
Centre for Marine and Coastal Policy, Marine Institute, Plymouth University

abstract_text: Sharks play an integral role in securing the health and productivity of the ocean. At the same time, they are very vulnerable to the pressures that we are exerting on the marine environment. With increasing evidence of the destructive impacts of human activities on marine ecosystems and key species groups such as sharks there is a growing call for stronger public engagement in marine governance. Knowledge and understanding of the issues as well as pro-environmental values are key elements that influence an individual’s behaviour and motivation to engage in conservation. This poster presents a study on public perceptions of sharks and shark conservation in the UK. The study investigated knowledge of and attitudes towards sharks of a group of individuals with a clear interest in the marine environment, as well as possible factors that might influence their perceptions of sharks, in order to make recommendations on how to foster shark conservation engagement. The key finding was that important prerequisites for engagement in shark conservation exist among parts of the UK public. The majority of respondents had good knowledge about sharks and positive, pro-conservation attitudes. However, this does not seem to be enough to motivate actual engagement. The study discusses a number of specific challenges with regard to sharks which might be influencing the way in which society connects to shark related issues.

title: Citizen science in shark conservation

authors.affiliation: The Shark Trust, UK

abstract_text: Citizen science – the involvement of volunteers in science - can be a useful tool in terms of engaging members of the public, raising awareness and aiding scientific data and information collection. To create effective protected areas and to better manage fisheries we need to know as much as possible about shark populations and movements. The Trust has a number of citizen science projects which contribute to this, including: The Great Eggcase Hunt was conceived as a way to raise public awareness of the presence and diversity of sharks, skates and rays in British waters, whilst also securing knowledge on the distribution of these species. The Angler Recording Project asks for elasmobranch catches to be recorded. Information collected for this project increases our understanding of inshore populations in the Southwest of England and will feed into more effective fisheries management and marine protected areas. The Basking Shark Project: Sightings and Photo-ID Databases store valuable information about this charismatic species, helping to map shark movements. Whilst providing easily accessible information, it must be recognised that citizen science does not provide a fully comprehensive dataset, as it relies on occasional finds/submissions rather than being survey-based. However once verified, information can become data and by harnessing modern technology and public enthusiasm for science, can increase the datasets available to the Trust for use in tangible conservation benefits.

title: Basking Shark Photo-ID Community Database

authors.affiliation: The Shark Trust, UK

abstract_text: Basking Sharks are seasonal visitors to the UK coastline, feeding on zooplankton at the sea surface during spring and summer months. These encounters provide researchers and enthusiastic amateurs with the perfect opportunity to photograph this normally elusive species. Photo-identification is a powerful, non-invasive field technique used for studying sharks in their natural environment. Many sharks display significant and recognisable markings on their fins, which can be natural (pigmentation) or acquired (injuries). These are used to identify individual sharks, allowing researchers to re-identify them between seasons. The Basking Shark Photo-ID project focuses on the development, population, maintenance and expansion of an online centralised community database, created in collaboration between The Shark Trust, Manx Basking Shark Watch, Marine Conservation International and the Irish Basking Shark Study Group. This community database (constructed by the Data Archive for Seabed Species (DASSH) team at the Marine Biological Association) is being used as a functional safe repository to store photo-identification data and images. Users can browse through uploaded images and search the catalogue by various fields (including characterising features, location, photographer etc.) to find individual sharks. Members of the public only have access to a limited view of the database, however partner organisations can register in order to gain access to additional information held on the full database. Unfortunately the project has suffered from a number of delays which have postponed the launch, however once these have been resolved the database will go live, allowing partners to browse, search and batch upload data.

abstract_text: The deep-sea shark genus Centrophorus is among the most confused taxa within Squaliformes. Historically, part of this confusion is attributable to ontogenetic changes that occur in its body shape throughout their life. Recent authors agree that only one species of Centrophorus inhabits the Mediterranean Sea. We describe here morphoanatomical changes in this species from specimens caught in the Balearic Sea. Indisputable evidence of existence of these changes arises from marked differences observed between pairs of specimens necessarily conspecific: full-term embryos and females that carry them. Thus we have tried fitting models to describe changes from full-term embryos/newborns (FTE&NB) to adults. Of 63 measurements analysed, 14,3% showed isometry, 36,5% positive allometry and 49,2% negative allometry. Negative allometry was found in most measurement related with head and tail. Positive allometry was generalised in measurements from pectoral and pelvic fins. Isometric or nearly isometric measurements were related with dorsal fins. Dermic denticles show marked changes in shape and size. FTE&NB have pointed acute denticles whereas adults show sessile blocklike denticles. General colour of body changes from gray in FTE&NB to brown in adults. Juveniles wear conspicuous withe margins in fins that disappear in adults. Major changes in dentition refer to number of asymmetric teeth in upper series. It increases from very few in FTE&NB to >10 in adults. Relevance of these changes for taxonomic purposes is discussed and some examples presented. Similar pattern of changes are expected to exist in other species of Centrophorus and should be considered for its morphoanatomical taxonomic characterisation.

abstract_text: The Velvet Belly Lanternshark Etmopterus spinax is a common deep-sea squaloid species distributed in the Eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. In the Gulf of Valencia it is commonly caught as bycatch by bottom trawling fishing vessels targeting for bathyal crustaceans. The species is classified as “Least concern” in the IUCN Red List. We compare here catches of E. spinax resulting from a studied series of fishing journeys carried out by bottom trawlers in the Gulf of Valencia (depth range = 430-790 m) in 1989 (n = 12) and in 2013 (n = 17). The purpose is to evaluate if relevant changes in the abundance or structure of the population have occurred, which could be related to fishing activity. Results show a moderate decrease in this time lapse both in frequency of occurrence (FO) and in mean number of specimens (MNS) caught per journey: FO 85,71% of journeys in 1989 and 76,47% of journeys in 2013; MNS: 4,93 ± 4,60 specimens/journey in 1989 and 3,88 ± 4,47 specimens/journey in 2013. However differences cannot be considered significant. In both years size frequency distribution of specimens was similar, including from newborns to adult specimens. Many of adult females caught were pregnant, mainly carrying from mid-term to full-term embryos. Several authors have pointed out for other geographic areas a marked decrease of abundance of E. spinax during last decades, attributing it to fishing pressure or environmental changes. Apparently this does not occur in the Gulf of Valencia but future monitoring studies are advisable.

abstract_text: Eight adult females of the rare Little Sleeper Shark Somniosus rostratus caught by bottom trawling fishing boats in the Balearic Sea were studied (550 - 670 m depth; size range 874 - 1042 mm TL). Five specimens had recognizable remains in its stomach contents, which corresponded in all cases to cephalopod beaks of mesopelagic squids Histioteuthis spp. This suggests that S. rostratus feeds mainly in the water column. From March to August 2013 a complete survey of catches at the Ibiza Channel (550-800 m depth) showed a mean catch rate of 5,81 * 10-2 specimens/journey (about 6,97 * 10-2 specimens/km2). abstract_text: The Angular Roughshark Oxynotus centrina is a poorly known demersal species that distributes in Eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. It is included in the IUCN Red List as Vulnerable at global scale but as Critically Endangered for the Mediterranean, although actually little is known about its biology, abundance or population dynamics. Direct observations of specimens in their habitat or cases of maintenance in aquaria are very scarce. We present here observations about feeding habits of a male specimen of O. centrina 40 cm TL caught in March 2013 at 150-200 depth in the Gulf of Valencia (Western Mediterranean) and kept in controlled conditions in aquaria. After unsuccessfully feeding attempts providing prey-items commonly found in field specimens stomachs according to bibliography (polychaete, molluscs, crustaceans), it was remarkable the predation on a ray egg when it was provided. Since then, feeding of this shark specimen has been managed successfully and regularly using eggs from several elasmobranch species. The procedure used to ingest the yolky-rich contents inside eggs cases by previously drilling their capsules was very similar in all cases, what suggests that it is not an incidental use of an prey item but a probable specialized behaviour. We hypothesize that feeding on elasmobranch eggs by O. centrina may have been partially overlooked due to the difficulty of identify yolk remains in stomach contents studies from field specimens. If this hypothesis is correct, relative abundance of oviparous elasmobranch species and their eggs could locally influence the trophic resources for this apparently threatened species.

abstract_text: The Smallspotted Catshark is one of the most abundant elasmobranchs in the Mediterranean Sea and the northeastern Atlantic. However, it is not known whether the species is represented by a single panmictic population or by different reproductively isolated populations. In the present study, a 590bp fragment of the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) COI gene region and 12 microsatellite loci were analyzed for 431 and 834 individuals respectively, in order to assess the genetic structure of the species. Samples originated from the eastern Mediterranean, the western Mediterranean and the Atlantic. Samples from the Atlantic and Egypt were included only in mtDNA analysis. The mtDNA median-joining network had a star-like shape and consisted of a central haplotype that was present in all regions, while the rest of the haplotypes had a clear geographical distribution and were found either in Atlantic and western Mediterranean or in eastern Mediterranean. Egypt was an exception as it contained haplotypes from both the aforementioned areas. Microsatellite as well as mtDNA analysis revealed a strong genetic differentiation and supported mainly the presence of two genetically distinct groups, one in the Eastern Mediterranean and another in the Western Mediterranean-Atlantic. There was also strong evidence for Isolation by Distance. The strong genetic and phylogeographic pattern found can be attributed to the low dispersal ability and the exclusively demersal lifestyle of the Smallspotted Catshark, which is mainly found in depths less than 500 m. It seems that the deep marine habitats are a strong barrier for the dispersal of this species.

abstract_text: The origin of a population of Great White Sharks (GWS), Carcharodon carcharias, L.1758, residing in the Mediterranean Sea has remained a mystery despite repeated scientific endeavours to retrace their history. Here we analyze 18 historical specimens (30-180 years old) collected from several museums, research institutes and private collections in Italy, creating the largest dataset of Mediterranean GWS mitochondrial DNA gene sequences (i.e. D-loop and COI). Comparative phylogenetic analyses of the Mediterranean GWS with populations from global range suggested a closer evolutionary relationship with sharks in Australia-New Zealand, Japan and the Pacific US rather than to the South-African population. Estimates of the most recent common ancestor carried out using internal calibration with fossil and paleo-geographical data revealed that Mediterranean GWS population originated in the early Pliocene at the end of the Messinian Salinity Crisis (ca. 5.3 MYA). This dating supports a GWS historical long-dispersal and paleo-colonization of the Mediterranean via a route of migration through Central America, before the formation of the Isthmus of Panama in contrast with a ad hoc previous hypothesis which suggested colonization via South Africa due to navigational errors during past climatic oscillations.

abstract_text: The oviducal gland, in oviparous cartilaginous fishes, plays the important role to produce the egg capsules containing fertilized eggs and to storage sperms in some species. To better understand the reproductive strategies of these animals, in this work we reported the first investigation on the macroscopical and microscopical structure of Raja miraletus’ oviducal gland from Sardinian waters (central western Mediterranean). Macroscopical analysis showed that the size of the oviducal gland increased with maturity reaching the largest width at the extruding stage, and having a consequent decline in regressing and regenerating ones. Histological study displayed that its development started at the maturing stage and completed at mature one. The previous analysis also permitted to discern the four zones composing the gland: club, papillary, baffle and terminal. Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) and alcian blue (AB) histochemical staining highlighted that the club zone stained AB+, PAS+ and AB+/PAS+; papillary showed a mixture of PAS+ and AB+; baffle seemed not react to this staining technique and the terminal zone was positive to AB and PAS near to the lumen. Furthermore, not aggregated sperms were observed in the secretory ducts of the baffle zone, near to the lamellae and the terminal zone. The histological measurements allowed, also, to observe an increase in size of the glandular area of each zone with maturity. Baffle zone, which has the task to form the egg capsule, represented the largest glandular zone in each stage reaching about 70% of the total area in mature females.

abstract_text: The Brazilian Sharpnose Shark Rhizoprionodon lalandii is a small coastal species (maximum length 80cm) widely distributed in the Western Atlantic from Panama to Uruguay. In Brazilian waters it is an important resource for artisanal fisheries, especially in south-east areas, representing 60% of the total shark landings. Nevertheless, the lack of ecological data on this species remains a critical issue to delineate management and conservation actions. Mortality rates were estimated using indirect methods based on life history parameters and direct methods (length-converted catch curves) based on length frequency of sharks caught by small-scale fisheries that operate along the south-central coast of São Paulo State, south-eastern Brazil, between 1997 and 2003. The total mortality (Z) values from indirect methods were 0.60 to 0.904, whereas catch curves produced values of 1.72 for females and 3.05 for males. Natural mortality (M) varied from 0.78 to 0.815 based on age-independent methods and from 1.24 (0 age) to 0.52 (7 years) based on age-dependent methods. Despite the range of estimates observed, the results reflect a high fishing pressure on a population that presents a high natural mortality. The fishing operation in a nursery ground for this species, using gill nets with small mesh sizes, has resulted in the capture of neonates right after birth. This scenario of overexploitation has been reported to governmental authorities as a means of contributing to the implementation of a regional marine protected area (corresponding to IUCN category V) management plan.

abstract_text: The use of photo identification (ID) has the potential to revolutionise elasmobranch research, enabling individual animals to be recognised and tracked over significant time periods. The Manx Basking Shark Watch has catalogued a minimum of 126 individual sharks from >5 years of photographic data collection. The differing injuries sustained by the dorsal fin, as used for individual identification, have been categorised and assessed. This dataset also provides new evidence for stock assessment, enabling the first estimate of Basking Shark population size in Manx waters. However, the discovery curve suggests this is a conservative estimate as the entire population has yet to be sampled. Within the catalogue, 71% of sharks display at least one type of human-inflicted injury, with the highest proportion of injuries (46%) caused by fishing nets. The data suggest that fin injury type is not significantly related to shark gender (Chi=8.73, CV=11.07, P<0.05), but is significantly related to shark size (Chi=66.6, CV=18.31, P<0.05). The photo-ID catalogue presents a non-intrusive form of mark/recapture data. Applying Schnabel's Index to our ‘well-marked’ catalogue (sharks with very distinct scars, notches etc.), estimates a population of 75 ‘well-marked’ sharks in Manx waters. These constitute 40.5% of our total catalogue, which equates to an estimated total population of 185 sharks. Given the small population size and wide prevalence of injuries, it is important that these data are considered in future management decisions. Suggested actions include speed limits in shark hotspots, further investigation into interactions with fishing gear and wide-scale collaborations to promote shark awareness.

title: Shark and other fish eye lenses – a window to cryptic life history behaviours

authors.affiliation: University of Southampton
University of Southampton
University of Southampton
University of Southampton

abstract_text: Traditionally, tagging studies provide information relating to the distribution and movement patterns of pelagic sharks. Electronic tags, however, are expensive, may have low return rates and cannot be attached to small juveniles. Incrementally grown tissues offer an alternative biochemical method to study ecology retrospectively. Otoliths, for example, contain a wealth of information pertaining to the age, growth and whole life, including juvenile, ecology of a species. The crystalline lens in the vertebrate eye also grows incrementally, but this structure has received relatively little analytical attention. Unlike otoliths, lenses are proteinaceous structures formed by fibre cell addition and subsequent progressive dehydration towards the core. They are acellular, and are not remodelled or replaced. Consequently, lenses have the potential to serve as a chronological record of biochemical information allowing examination of ontogenetic movement patterns, migration and juvenile ecology in a wide range of functional groups, including elasmobranchs. Here we report pilot data examining the dietary ecology and movement/migration of the Porbeagle Shark Lamna nasus using stable isotope analyses from sequential samples of eye lens tissue. We explore the potential for eye lenses as a log of life-long diet and spatial ecology, and compare their role as biochemical host tissues with vertebrae. We use the recovered diet and migration data to reconstruct feeding and movement ecology in juvenile Porbeagle Sharks and compare inferences from stable isotope data with those from physical tagging.

abstract_text: Although the Nurse Shark, Ginglymostoma cirratum, is listed as endangered in Brazil (IN05-2004), it is commonly caught by artisanal fishing in Brazilian northeast coast. In the present study, uterine samples of ten females were collected from nurse sharks landed in Mucuripe beach, at Ceara State (Latitude e longitude), being then processed to routine histology with HE, PAS and Alcian Blue 2.5% staining. The morphometry of the body and reproductive tract was conducted to the nearest centimeter. The macroscopic maturity stage was defined, according to literature. All females were immature. The uteri of the nurse sharks examined contained three (03) layers: mucous, muscular and serous. The uterine mucosae were internally lined by a simple columnar epithelium. An undeveloped lamina propria line was present just below the epithelium, and it consisted of loose connective tissue with blood and lymph vessels. Uterine glands were not observed. In the middle portion of the uterus, a stratified epithelium with papiliform projections and alcian blue positive were present. The muscle and serosa layers were similar to those of other elasmobranch species. The presence of vascularized epithelium, mucous cells, and an acellular collagen PAS positive layer under the epithelium line are uterine mucosa specializations which allow the uterus to provide a stable physiological environment to G. cirratum embryos, after they have broken out of the egg case. These histological findings indicate that despite the lecithothrophic viviparity of the species, the uterus wall has an important role in embryo survivorship.

title: Supporting sustainable shark, skate and ray fisheries in Northern English waters

authors.affiliation: The Shark Trust, UK

abstract_text: In recent decades landings of elasmobranchs by the Northern English fleet have reduced considerably in volume and are now largely taken as bycatch. Nevertheless elasmobranchs continue to represent a commercially valuable component within mixed fisheries. In 2012, with funding from the Co-operative Foundation Environment Fund, the Shark Trust commenced a project engaging with the commercial fishing industry in Northern England. The aim of the project is to support the industry in maintaining and profiting from well-managed, sustainable elasmobranch fisheries. The Shark Trust has a solid track record in working with the commercial fishing industry towards sustainable fisheries; however this has largely centred on the Southwest of England, home to the major UK elasmobranch landing ports. This project shifts the focus to Northern England, a region with a long shark fishing heritage. Key project objectives include developing a positive relationship with the industry, supporting accuracy in elasmobranch identification and aiding compliance with regulations applicable to a growing number of species. As catch and landings data continue to improve, those stocks able to support sustainable fisheries can be more effectively managed, while those showing greatest declines can benefit from more bespoke protective measures and might again, in time, support well-managed fisheries. The Shark Trust has liaised widely with all sectors of the Northern English fishing industry to assess interest in the project and ensure relevance and practicality of supporting materials.

title: Results from the Shark Trust’s Angler Recording Project

authors.affiliation: The Shark Trust, UK

abstract_text: Distribution and abundance data are fundamental in establishing sustainable elasmobranch fisheries in the Northeast Atlantic. As well as scientific sources, useful data can also come from ‘citizen science’ projects. In 2010 the Shark Trust initiated the Angler Recording Project, encouraging sea-anglers in the Southwest of England to record and share details of their elasmobranch catches. To-date, over 1500 catch records have been submitted by sea-anglers. These range from the pelagic Porbeagle Shark Lamna nasus to the demersal Smallspotted Catshark Scyliorhinus canicula; and from the larger-bodied Blonde Ray Raja brachyura to the smaller, faster growing Spotted Ray R. montagui. For all species, fishing effort – as opposed to natural abundance and/or population trends – must be considered the key driver of results at present. Half of all records submitted have come from Cornish waters; although falling outside the project boundary, South Wales also features prominently, ining records for a significant number of pelagic sharks known to move throughout the Bristol Channel and Celtic Sea marine areas. Commercial charter vessels and sea-angling clubs accounted for more than 80% of catch records submitted, a bias reflected in the project’s overall catch composition, with the Blue Shark Prionace glauca the most frequently recorded elasmobranch – and also the primary target for most charter operations. The Blonde Ray is the most commonly recorded batoid. Key challenges arising include maintaining interest in the project and the flow of data. Similarly, the project has experienced difficulties in engaging unaffiliated (to a sea-angling club or similar organisation) anglers who make up approximately 75% of all sea-anglers.

It’s particularly the case for species that seems to have patchy coastal distribution which are not well sampled by the scientific fishery-independent surveys. Information on the mixing between skates of different areas and the populations structures but also on biology and possible movements between ecologically important grounds are needed for management purposes. The French RECOAM project was set up in 2012 to contribute to a better knowledge of five skate species, Undulate Ray Raja undulata, Blonde Ray Raja brachyura, Smalleyed Ray Raja microocellata, Thornback Ray Raja clavata and Spotted Ray Raja montagui, working in two areas of the French waters of particular interest, one in the western English Channel and one in the Bay of Biscay. The aims of the project are to investigate the populations’ structures, to enhance the understanding of skates’ movements which could contribute to identify important grounds in their life cycles, and to evaluate the length at maturity for each species, a fundamental parameter given its importance in the assessment models. We present here the project progress and some preliminary results, particularly concerning the Undulate Ray Raya undulata tagging results and length at maturity.

title: Philopatric behaviour in Northeast Atlantic Spurdog Squalus acanthias, a Critically Endangered elasmobranch

abstract_text: Philopatric behaviour is increasingly recognised as a common feature of several elasmobranch populations globally; identification and incorporation of this behaviour into conservation plans has the potential to substantially increase the effectiveness of localised static management for highly mobile species. Spurdog Squalus acanthias, a small, critically endangered elasmobranch, has been shown to display philopatric behaviour in other parts of its global distribution, but not within the NE Atlantic. Here we report findings from a multiannual mark/recapture study along with results collected over a year from a static acoustic curtain and archival tag research programme within Loch Etive on the west coast of Scotland. Mark/recapture data suggests spurdog of both sexes are present in the loch throughout the year, potentially indicating a resident component within Etive. Observational data also support the presence of breeding and neonatal Spurdog within the loch at different times of the year. Building on this, the data storage tags and acoustic curtain revealed mature female Spurdog move out of the loch over winter, returning to the loch in spring time; behaviour previously unrecorded in NE Atlantic Spurdog. This philopatric behaviour suggests that spatial management of Loch Etive would effectively aid conservation of different age and sex classes of Spurdog.

title: Implementation of the European Plan of Action for the Conservation and Management of Sharks

authors.affiliation: Dutch Elasmobranch Association
Dutch Elasmobranch Association

abstract_text: In 2009 the European Commission has issued a European Community Plan of Action for the Conservation and Management of sharks (the CPOA). In addition to mandatory actions for Regional Fisheries Management Organizations and Member States as part of the European Community, this policy plan contains recommendations for voluntary national measures Member States can implement to address the data gaps for elasmobranch species and their role in the ecosystem, to improve the knowledge about their fisheries, To ensure more sustainable fisheries and regulation of bycatch, and to ensure a coherent approach in policy. In this study it was assessed to what extent the CPOA has been implemented by the North Sea countries and what should still be undertaken to restore and protect the North Sea elasmobranch species. After reviewing the current protection status of species in the area, the gaps in biological knowledge necessary for proper management and conservation are addressed for each species. Subsequently, the implementation of possible voluntary measures are assessed, leading up to recommendations on necessary action.
